title: Maryland Supreme Court blocks suit by woman who was shot on Towson campus
summary: A Towson University alumna who was shot at an on-campus party in 2021 cannot sue the university for failing to protect her in the incident, after the Maryland Supreme Court dismissed her case this week.
content:
by Rhiannon Evans, Maryland Matters April 23, 2026

by Rhiannon Evans, Maryland Matters April 23, 2026

A Towson University alumna who was shot at an on-campus party in 2021 cannot sue the university for failing to protect her in the incident, after the Maryland Supreme Court dismissed her case this week.

The court, after considering briefs and oral arguments from both parties in Catherine Torney’s case, said in a one-page order Tuesday that it shouldn’t have taken the case up in the first place. The order lets stand lower court rulings that had dismissed Torney’s case.

“The one-line order that says, ‘We decided not to decide,’ doesn’t tell you much,” said Torney’s attorney, Joseph Cammarata.

Torney was one of hundreds who flocked to Towson University’s Freedom Square on the night of Sept. 3, 2021. The unsanctioned party quickly swelled from 100 to roughly 400 people by midnight.

Campus police officers on the scene alerted their superiors to the situation, but got no response from the Towson University Police Department, so the party went on, according to court documents.

Around 2 a.m. Torney was shot alongside two others. The gunman was never identified.

In 2023, Torney sued the university, claiming that it was negligent in its duty to protect her from “foreseeable harm” while on university grounds. Torney also argued that the university had insufficiently trained and supervised its campus police officers.

The university moved to dismiss the case, and a circuit judge agreed. That ruling was upheld by the Appellate Court of Maryland, which said that “a noisy, large gathering of young people, even one that includes arguments among the attendees, is insufficient to signal that violence might be imminent.”

The appeals court also said that there were no opportunities for campus police to try to prevent the shooting since there was no prior shooting allegation or knowledge of a weapon being present at the gathering before shots were fired.

Torney then took her case to the state Supreme Court, which decided in January to hear the case. Oral arguments took place earlier this month.

Torney’s legal team argued that campus police should have stepped in once the gathering grew large and unruly.

“The university wants to change the definition of foreseeability,” Cammarata said during oral arguments on April 9. “They want to eliminate the F-O-R and just make it ‘seeability.’”

The university’s attorneys argued that there were no signs that anyone at the “pop-up party” was armed or dangerous, according to court documents.

“[Campus police] didn’t know anyone was armed at the party,” said Assistant Attorney General Ryan Dietrich, arguing on behalf of Towson University. “And then they didn’t know that there was violence that was impending or imminent.”

Torney, who had been asking for a jury trial, will not get another day in court now and the lower court rulings will stand.

“It’s disappointing. We would have liked a decision on the merits,” Cammarata said.

Towson University officials referred questions about the case to the Maryland Attorney General’s office, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday.
